title: She was already dead.
paragraphs: And everyone in the room knew it.

No pulse.
No breath.
No hope.
That’s the part we skip too fast.
Because when you stand in a room filled with loss—real loss, not theory—you either perform… or you fall to your knees.
Because he knew something we forget when shame is loud and failure feels final.

There are moments where talking won’t fix it.
Explaining won’t fix it.
Trying harder won’t fix it.
Some things only move… when God moves.
Acts 9 doesn’t give us a polished miracle story. It gives us tension.

Widows crying.
Clothes in their hands—evidence of Tabitha’s kindness.
A body laid still in an upper room.
And then Peter walks in—not as a hero—but as a desperate man who knows his limits.
Before resurrection came… surrender came first.
Before power was displayed… dependence was chosen.
Before the miracle… there was a man admitting, “God, if You don’t move, nothing will.”
That’s where many of us break.
Because we don’t like that place.
We like hiding the fact that inside, something in us has already died.

Dead passion.
Dead purity.
Dead prayer life.
Dead hunger for God.
And we cover it up with activity, with church language, with filtered faith.
But God is not moved by performance.
“But Peter put them all outside, knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, ‘Tabitha, arise.’ And she opened her eyes…” — Acts 9:40
He didn’t start with the miracle.
Some scholars interpret this moment as Peter intentionally following the pattern of Jesus in Mark 5:40–41—removing the noise, creating space, depending fully on the Father.
Because real power is not imitation.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Tabitha wasn’t raised because she was famous.
She was known for good works. Quiet service. Hidden love.
Faithfulness does not exempt you from broken moments.
You can serve, love, give… and still face loss.
So what do you do when your life doesn’t match your obedience?
When you did right… but it still fell apart?
When you prayed… but it still died?
This is where shame creeps in.

“Maybe I failed God.”
“Maybe I’m not enough.”
“Maybe this is the end.”
Death is not always the end of the story.
Because the same Jesus who empowered Peter in that room is the One who walked into our greatest problem—sin—and didn’t just visit it…
“...you were dead in your trespasses and sins…” — Ephesians 2:1
No ability to fix ourselves. No power to resurrect our own hearts.
But Jesus didn’t stand at a distance.

He lived the life we couldn’t live.
Died the death we deserved.
Took the weight of sin, shame, and judgment on the cross.
“Christ died for our sins… He was buried… He was raised on the third day…” — 1 Corinthians 15:3–4
Because now, resurrection is not just something God does.
So when Peter said, “Tabitha, arise,” it wasn’t Peter’s power.
It was borrowed authority from a risen Savior.
And that same Jesus is still speaking today.
To secret sin you thought no one knew.
To that quiet failure you buried under “I’m fine.”
From sin. From self. From control.
Not when you clean yourself up.
But when you finally admit you can’t.
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” — James 4:6
What in your life feels dead right now?

Your prayer life?
Your purity?
Your calling?
Your closeness with God?
Because the same Christ who raised from the grave is not intimidated by your condition.
He’s inviting you out of it.
Call on Him before you quit.
And watch what God does with what you thought was over.
